newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN to demand explanation of Israeli torture ruling.
newsitem.headline: UN to demand explanation of Israeli torture ruling.

text.p: The United Nations Committee against Torture, concerned that an Israeli court ruling might violate an international human rights treaty, plans to ask the government for an explanation, U.N. sources said on Friday.

Israel's High Court overturned on Thursday an interim court order which had forbidden Israel's Shin Bet secret police to use "physical force" against a Palestinian detainee, according to a courts spokesman.

"The committee has taken up the question. There was surprise and concern upon learning of the ruling from news reports and I think the committee will do something so the government provides an explanation," a U.N. source told Reuters.
"The members are still discussing the modalities of their approach, but they want all the necessary information," he said.
Members were eager to see the text of the ruling and planned to send a request in written form to the government, according to the U.N. source.
"If news reports are true, it sounds like institutionalising torture. That would be very serious," he said.

The U.N. committee of 10 independent experts, who are holding their semi-annual session in Geneva, oversee compliance with the 1987 Convention against Torture which has 100 state parties. Israel ratified it in 1991 but said it could not accept articles which could allow the body to make a special inquiry.
Earlier, Peter Burns, a Canadian professor who is a senior member of the body and its rapporteur (investigator) for Israel, said the court decision risked sanctioning torture of detainees.
"It is very disappointing that the Israeli supreme court would legitimise the use of even moderate physical force in interrogating suspected terrorists," Burns told Reuters.
"It is particularly disappointing that such a civilised society as Israel should feel the need to resort to such measures even in the face of imminent danger," he added.
"We do not see how, in the middle of an investigation, an interrogator can ensure that moderate physical pressure does not become torture," Burns said.

"There is a real risk in every interrogation where moderate physical pressure is used, it could slip into conduct which amounts to torture especially if they have a suspected terrorist and they are convinced he has information on an impending major attack."
In Israel, a court spokesman said the ruling allowed the security services to use the necessary force to get the information they needed to advance an investigation.
Israeli media reports said the detainee was a member of the militant Islamic Jihad group and had information about attacks planned against Israeli targets.

Israel had been due to file a regular report to the U.N. committee on its compliance with the convention by November 1, but none has been received so far, according to U.N. sources. The report normally would be discussed at the session in April.

A 1987 Israeli commission ruled the Shin Bet could use "moderate physical pressure" in interrogations and "increased physical pressure" when an attack was imminent. Human rights groups have said the commission's report sanctioned torture.

Israel has been on high alert for a possible Islamic Jihad suicide attack to mark the anniversary of the assassination of the group's leader, Fathi Shqaqi, in Malta last year. Shqaqi's killers were never caught but Palestinians blame Israel.
The Islamic Jihad has claimed responsibility for suicide attacks in Israel which left scores of people dead.
